coach_says: You were already worse here and Ne2 is about as good as the alternatives; Nd5, centralising the knight, was a touch more active. Nothing in this move is a real mistake to learn from; the problems came earlier when your king got exposed.
Nd5 is the best move: it hits the f6 knight that guards your g5 bishop's target and lets you win back material after Nxf6+. Well spotted, keep looking for moves that attack a defender.

Your queen had to leave h5, and Qh3 keeps an eye on the e6 pawn almost as well as Qe2 does. The difference between the two is small; the important thing was not to leave the queen where gxh5 takes it.
Rf2 blocks the check sensibly and is close to the engine's choices of moving the king. You were already in trouble from the earlier lost pawns; this move didn't change much.
Castling queenside protects the d7 pawn from the rook on g7 and brings your rook to the centre, which is a reasonable practical choice. The engine's alternatives are only marginally better.
This bishop ending is difficult whatever you play, and a5 is about as good as the other moves. Nothing here a coach would stop on.

Your queen had to move because Rf1 attacked it, but Qg6 sends it to the edge where Nf4 hits it again with tempo. Qe4 was much stronger: from the centre it attacks the e2 knight and adds pressure on d4 together with your b6 bishop. When the queen has to move, look for the square where it does the most work and can't be chased straight away.

White has pushed f3 and g4 and his king is still on e1, so this is the moment to open the centre with c5. That strikes at d4 and, after cxd4 and ...d4 or ...Nc6, your pieces flood towards an uncastled king. c6 is too passive and gives White time to finish developing. When your opponent attacks on the wing with his king in the middle, hit back in the centre.

Qh4 attacks the f6 rook, but your queen on h4 has no protection and sits on the same diagonal as Black's queen on e7. Black simply trades both rooks on f1 with check, the f6 rook leaves the diagonal and Qxh4 wins your queen. Before putting a piece on a square, check what lines open after the forced exchanges; here Rxf6 first was clean and kept your advantage.

Your rook on d5 was attacked by the c4 bishop, and Nc2 ignored that. White takes Bxd5 exd5, saves his own rook with Rc1, and you have just lost the exchange while your knight is stuck on c2. Deal with the attack first: Rc5 moves the rook with tempo by hitting the bishop. A counter-attack only works if your threat is bigger than theirs and they can't answer it with a simple move.

Your e5 pawn was attacked three times (d7 and c6 knights, g7 bishop) and defended only twice. After castling, Black plays Ndxe5 Nxe5 Qxd1, trading queens on the open d-file with tempo, and then picks up e5 for free. Count attackers and defenders before a quiet move; Qe2 took the queen off the d-file so the trade on e5 no longer worked, and tactics on f7 kept Black from grabbing it.
also: queens facing on an open file

coach_says: Your rook on f5 is out in front of your pawns with very few safe squares. After Bd7, White plays dxe5 dxe5 and then g4, and the rook has nowhere good to go: Rf8 runs into Bxg5 and Rf6 into Nxe5, so you have to give it up for the knight. The engine's ...g4 yourself takes that square away from White first. When a rook comes out early, check whether a pawn can chase it into a corner.

Nd7 lets White swap knight for bishop with Bxd7, and the pawn ending after Kxd7 is lost: White's king walks to h6, and his f and h pawns run while your king is far away on the queenside. Before allowing a trade into a king and pawn ending, count it out; the extra pawn means nothing if the enemy king is the active one. Keeping the knight with Nb3 or Ne6 kept you winning.
concept: trading into a lost pawn ending

coach_says: The bishop on a6 was attacking your rook on f1. Instead of solving that, Rxf7 gave the rook away for one pawn, and Black's king is not exposed enough to justify it. d3 was simple: it blocks the bishop's diagonal and opens the way for your c1 bishop at the same time. When a piece is attacked, look for a block that also develops before reaching for a sacrifice.
also: block the attack with a developing move

coach_says: Your back rank is weak: your rook on a8 and bishop on c8 are still at home and White owns the open d-file. While your knight was on e5 it could cover d7, but Nxc4 takes it away, and Rd8+ Bf8 Bh6 leaves you unable to stop Rxf8 mate. Before grabbing material, check the checks your opponent gets, especially along an open file to your back rank. Developing with Bg4 kept everything safe.

You could have just taken the bishop with Qxb3. It looks protected by the a2 pawn, but that pawn is pinned: if axb3, your rook on a8 would be giving check down the open a-file, so the recapture is illegal. Whenever a piece is defended by a pawn, check whether that pawn is pinned to the king. Qf3 left you a piece down.

Your bishop on e4 was attacked twice, and d5 props it up but lets White trade it off with Nxe4 dxe4. That swaps your best piece and leaves your c4 and e4 pawns isolated and weak. Just retreat with Bb7: from the long diagonal it eyes g2, and with Qg5 and Ra3 you keep real pressure on White's king and e3. Keep a strong bishop rather than defending it in a way that invites the trade.

White's queen on c7 is deep in your camp with almost no squares, and e5 traps it: it opens your f8 bishop to cover d6 and e7, and ...Ne8 next wins the queen for a knight. Bg4 moved the bishop off c8, so the queen escaped with Qxb7. When the enemy queen grabs pawns in your position, count its escape squares and look for a move that takes the last ones away.

Black has just taken on d4 and the natural move is to take it back with Nxd4, putting your knight in the centre. Ng5 moves the same piece twice and attacks nothing, since f7 is well defended without your bishop on c4, and after ...Be7 the knight just has to go back while you're a pawn down. In the opening, recapture your pawn and develop before going on raids.
also: moving a piece twice in the opening

coach_says: Nc6 hits the queen, but after Qc5 the knight is loose and you have to trade down. Qxb5 was there: the a6 pawn can't take back, because axb5 opens the a-file and Rxa8+ wins the rook, and then the queen that blocks on d8 too. When a pawn defends something, check whether moving it would open a line onto a piece behind it.
